title: Indexes
summary: How a B-tree index finds one row among a billion in a handful of reads, and what every index costs.

blocks.p: A users table stores rows in no order that helps a search by email. To find the user with a given email, the database has no choice but to read every row and compare. That is a **full table scan**.
With 1,000 rows, nobody notices. With 100 million rows, every login reads 100 million rows. The query that was instant in testing takes seconds in production.

An **index** is a separate structure, kept sorted by one or more columns, that points to the rows. Most databases use a **B-tree** by default. It is a tree of fixed-size pages. Each page holds many sorted keys and pointers to the pages below, so the tree is wide and shallow.
To find a key, the database reads the root page, picks the child whose range contains the key, and repeats until it reaches a leaf. The leaf points to the row.

blocks.caption: Finding one email in a table of 96 rows. The scan reads every row, because another row could match. The index reads one page per level, then the row.

blocks.p: Each page holds hundreds of keys. If each page points to 100 children, three levels cover a million rows and five levels cover more than a billion. Doubling the table adds a fraction of a level.

list: **Slower writes.** Every insert, update or delete must also update each index on the table.
**Space.** An index is a copy of the indexed columns, plus pointers.
**Only some queries benefit.** An index on `email` helps `WHERE email = ?` and range or prefix queries on email. It doesn't help a query that filters on another column.

**B-tree is the default.** In PostgreSQL, `CREATE INDEX` builds a B-tree unless you ask for another type. The [index types page](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-types.html) lists the operators each type supports.

**Column order matters in a multicolumn index.** An index on `(country, city)` works best for queries on country, or on country and city. A query on city alone can't jump straight to its rows. Since version 18, PostgreSQL can sometimes use the index anyway with a skip scan, which works well when there are few distinct countries. PostgreSQL's [multicolumn index page](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html) explains both.
**Check the plan.** `EXPLAIN` shows whether the database will use an index or scan the table. See PostgreSQL's [guide to EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html).
**Index for your queries.** Add an index for each slow, frequent query, and remove indexes that no query uses.

blocks.p: Change the size of the table and see how the page reads grow for a scan and for an index with 100 keys per page. Both sides assume 100 rows or keys fit in one page.

blocks.caption: Pages a scan reads, against pages an index lookup reads. Go from a thousand rows to a billion.

list: Without an index, finding a row means reading the whole table.
A B-tree index is a wide, shallow tree of sorted pages.
Each level multiplies the rows covered by the number of keys per page, so lookups stay short.
Every index slows writes and uses space, so add the ones your queries need.
